text: Farm records are useful for a Preah Vihear smallholder because livestock can generate income through meat, live-animal sales, eggs, milk, breeding animals, or manure, often simultaneously. Record the number/type of animals, births/hatchings, deaths, purchases, sales, feed quantities and costs, veterinary expenses, vaccination dates, major health problems, labor, and major housing/equipment costs. For cattle, record body condition/weight, breeding, calving, illness, deaths, and purchase/sale details. For pigs, record litter size, piglet deaths, growth, feed use, illness, and finishing/sale weight. For chickens and ducks, flock-level records (mortality, feed, egg production, age at sale, sale price) are usually more realistic than individual-bird records. The key calculation is net income/profit, not just money received at sale — a large sale price can still mean a loss once feed, transport, mortality, medicine, and market fees are subtracted. Records also function as an early-warning system: a normal 80 eggs/week dropping suddenly to 45 with reduced feed intake and deaths is a health signal, not just a production number. During the wet season (roughly May–October) and dry season (roughly November–April), record actual conditions (heavy rain, flooding, heat stress, water shortages, disease events) so the farmer can compare seasonal performance rather than assuming every season behaves the same. A simple notebook is sufficient — computerized systems, individual electronic ID, and precise labor-hour accounting are not necessary minimums for a smallholder. No specific breed or variety should be guessed for Preah Vihear livestock; record what the farmer actually has.
